New machine. Its objects are: vesoso, mekukil, kanago, denasa, gumusu, vinatir.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects together to see how the machine reacts.

TEST: vesoso, mekukil, kanago
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group of three did not light up. If any single nexiom is enough to light the machine, then the two nexioms must both be among the other three objects. If both nexioms must be present together, they could be split between the groups. Testing the other three together will help separate these possibilities.

TEST: denasa, gumusu, vinatir
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Both nexioms must be among denasa, gumusu and vinatir.

- **If any single nexiom lights the machine:** the first group had no nexioms, so both are in the second group.
- **If both nexioms must be present:** the second group lit, so it held both.
- **If exactly one nexiom must be present:** that cannot fit both results. The second group would need exactly one nexiom, putting the other in the first group, which then should have lit.

So the open questions are which pair it is and which of the first two rules applies. Testing denasa alone helps with both. If it lights, a single nexiom is enough and denasa is one. If it doesn't, either denasa is not a nexiom or the machine needs both together.

TEST: denasa
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

If a single nexiom is enough to light the machine, denasa failing alone rules it out. The pair would then have to be gumusu and vinatir. If both nexioms must be present together, any pair among denasa, gumusu and vinatir is still possible.

Testing gumusu alone separates these cases:
- **If it lights:** a single nexiom is enough, and the nexioms are gumusu and vinatir.
- **If it doesn't:** the machine needs both nexioms together. My remaining two tests can then check pairs to find the right one.

TEST: gumusu
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

A single nexiom cannot be enough to light the machine. If it were, denasa failing would make gumusu a nexiom, but gumusu failed alone too. So the machine needs both nexioms present together, and the pair is one of three: denasa and gumusu, denasa and vinatir, or gumusu and vinatir.

I'll test denasa with gumusu. If it lights, that's the pair. If not, one more test of denasa with vinatir will decide between the last two.

TEST: denasa, gumusu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

The machine only lights when both nexioms are present together.
- **Any single nexiom is enough:** ruled out, because both denasa and gumusu failed alone, so the pair would have no members left.
- **Exactly one nexiom must be present:** ruled out after the first two tests, since the first group would have needed to light.

With both nexioms required, denasa and gumusu lighting together means they are the pair. Any pair with a non-nexiom would not have lit. My last test isn't needed.

ANSWER: nexioms = denasa, gumusu
One last question. If only denasa were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No. I already tested denasa alone in my third test, and the machine did not light up. That fits the rule I found: the machine lights only when both nexioms, denasa and gumusu, are present together, so denasa by itself is not enough.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: muvafi, bukuvis, digamok, kakubur, gukamor, vamenil.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects together to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: muvafi, bukuvis, digamok
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The first three objects together did not light the machine. Under an "any nexiom lights it" rule, both nexioms would then be among the other three. Under other rules, such as "needs both nexioms," that result tells us less. Testing the other three together will help separate these cases.

TEST: kakubur, gukamor, vamenil
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither XOR nor "exactly one" fits both results, since one of the two tests would have gone the other way. The rule is most likely "any nexiom lights it" (OR) or "needs both" (AND). Under either rule, both nexioms are among kakubur, gukamor and vamenil. Testing a pair from that group will help separate the remaining options.

TEST: kakubur, gukamor
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Both earlier tests that lit up contain nexioms, and the first group of three apparently has none. So the nexioms are most likely two of kakubur, gukamor and vamenil.

- **If any nexiom lights the machine:** the pair could be kakubur–gukamor, kakubur–vamenil or gukamor–vamenil. All three fit, since each includes kakubur or gukamor.
- **If it needs both nexioms:** the pair must be kakubur–gukamor.

Testing vamenil alone separates these cases:
- **If it stays dark:** vamenil is not a nexiom, so the answer is kakubur–gukamor under either rule.
- **If it lights up:** vamenil is a nexiom, and testing kakubur alone will settle the second one.

TEST: vamenil
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Taken together, the four results point to kakubur and gukamor.

- **Rule:** "Exactly one nexiom" and XOR can't explain the results. That leaves "any nexiom lights it" (OR) or "needs both nexioms" (AND) as the simple rules that fit.
- **Group:** Under either rule, the first test (muvafi, bukuvis, digamok) stayed dark, so the nexioms are among kakubur, gukamor and vamenil.
- **Vamenil:** Vamenil alone stayed dark, so it is not a nexiom under either rule.
- **Answer:** That leaves kakubur and gukamor. This matches kakubur and gukamor lighting the machine together.

One unusual rule, "lights only when no nexioms are present," would also fit the results and point to a different pair. I'm treating it as unlikely, and the two remaining tests couldn't fully resolve it anyway.

ANSWER: nexioms = kakubur, gukamor
One last question. If only gukamor were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

My tests never separated the two rules that fit the data, so this is a guess between them.

- **If any nexiom lights the machine (OR):** gukamor alone would light it up.
- **If it needs both nexioms (AND):** gukamor alone would stay dark.

Every lit test contained both kakubur and gukamor, and every dark test contained neither. A test of kakubur or gukamor alone would have settled it, but I didn't run one. I lean slightly towards "any nexiom lights it" because it is the simpler rule. That is a judgement call, not something the results showed.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: mubupul, limurus, fokipen, sukoren, nifugi, meposik.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: mubupul, limurus, fokipen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

Nothing lit with the first three, so I'll test the other three to see whether the machine responds at all.

TEST: sukoren, nifugi, meposik
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Since the first three never lit the machine and the other three did, both nexioms are probably among sukoren, nifugi and meposik. The machine might light when any nexiom is present, or only when both are. Testing sukoren and nifugi one at a time should tell those rules apart and identify the pair.

TEST: sukoren
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Sukoren alone did not light the machine. If any single nexiom lights it, sukoren is not a nexiom and the pair is nifugi and meposik. If it only lights when both are present, the pair could be any two of sukoren, nifugi and meposik. Testing nifugi and meposik together should settle most of this: if it lights, they are the pair under either rule.

TEST: nifugi, meposik
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Under an "any nexiom lights it" rule, nifugi and meposik failing together means neither is a nexiom. Sukoren also failed alone, so the three would never have lit the machine together, which they did. That rule is ruled out.

A "lights only when both nexioms are present" rule fits all four results:
- No pair lies entirely within mubupul, limurus and fokipen.
- Both nexioms lie within sukoren, nifugi and meposik.
- Nifugi and meposik are not the pair, so sukoren must be a nexiom.

That leaves two candidates: sukoren with nifugi, or sukoren with meposik. Testing sukoren and nifugi together will decide between them.

TEST: sukoren, nifugi
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Every possible pair can be checked against the five results.

- **Both nexioms among mubupul, limurus, fokipen:** Test 2 would have lit with no nexioms present. Test 3 (sukoren) also had no nexioms and did not light, so this is impossible.
- **One nexiom on each side:** The nexiom among sukoren, nifugi, meposik lit the machine by itself in test 2. But each of those three was tested in a set holding no other nexiom (tests 3 and 4), and none lit. So this is impossible.
- **Both nexioms among sukoren, nifugi, meposik:**
  - Sukoren and nifugi fails, because test 5 held both and did not light.
  - Nifugi and meposik fails, because test 4 held both and did not light.
  - Sukoren and meposik fits every result. The machine lit only when both were present (test 2), and no test held just one of them and lit.

The pair must be sukoren and meposik, so I don't need the last test.

ANSWER: nexioms = sukoren, meposik
One last question. If only meposik were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No. It would not light up.

The deciding result is test 4. Nifugi and meposik together did not light the machine. Nifugi is not a nexiom, and objects that aren't nexioms never affect the machine. So that test was effectively meposik on its own, and it stayed dark. Meposik alone would behave the same way.

This fits the rule the results point to: the machine lights only when both nexioms, sukoren and meposik, are present together.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: tegofa, gizapas, rivoda, rasemen, norupen, ditilu.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: tegofa, gizapas, rivoda
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

Nothing lit with tegofa, gizapas and rivoda, but I don't yet know the rule (one nexiom enough, both needed, or something else). Testing the other three should help narrow it down.

TEST: rasemen, norupen, ditilu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Since tegofa, gizapas and rivoda didn't light the machine but rasemen, norupen and ditilu did, both nexioms are most likely in the second group. That holds whether one nexiom is enough or both are needed. Testing rasemen alone will start to separate the possibilities.

TEST: rasemen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Ruling out the possible rules and pairs so far:

- **"At least one nexiom lights it":** test 1 means none of tegofa, gizapas or rivoda are nexioms. Test 3 rules out rasemen. That leaves **norupen and ditilu**.
- **"Both nexioms are needed":** test 2 puts both nexioms among rasemen, norupen and ditilu. Rasemen failing alone tells us nothing, so any pair from those three is possible.
- **"Exactly one nexiom lights it":** this can't fit. For test 2 to light, exactly one nexiom would have to be in the second group. The other would then sit alone in the first group, and test 1 would have lit.

Testing norupen alone separates these. If it lights, the rule is "at least one," and the answer is norupen and ditilu. If it doesn't, the rule is "both needed," and I'll test pairs next.

TEST: norupen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Norupen alone did not light. That rules out "at least one nexiom lights it," because then norupen would have been a nexiom and lit by itself. So the rule must be that **both nexioms are needed**.

From test 2, both nexioms are among rasemen, norupen and ditilu, which leaves three possible pairs:
- rasemen + norupen
- rasemen + ditilu
- norupen + ditilu

I'll test rasemen with norupen. If it lights, that's the pair. If not, one more test (rasemen with ditilu) will settle which of the other two pairs it is.

TEST: rasemen, norupen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Rasemen with norupen did not light, so that pair is ruled out. Under the "both needed" rule, the nexioms are either rasemen + ditilu or norupen + ditilu. Testing rasemen with ditilu settles it: if it lights, those two are the nexioms; if not, the answer is norupen and ditilu.

TEST: rasemen, ditilu
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Rasemen with ditilu did not light either, so that pair is ruled out too.

Here is how all six results fit together:
- Tests 1 and 2 put both nexioms among rasemen, norupen and ditilu.
- Norupen failing alone (test 4) means one nexiom is not enough, so both must be present.
- Of the three possible pairs, rasemen + norupen (test 5) and rasemen + ditilu (test 6) both failed.

That leaves **norupen and ditilu** as the only pair that fits every result under the "both needed" rule. This assumes the rule is one of the simple ones I considered. "At least one" and "exactly one" are ruled out by the results, and a more unusual rule wasn't directly tested.

ANSWER: nexioms = norupen, ditilu
One last question. If only ditilu were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**No**, under the rule I inferred. Ditilu alone was never tested, so this rests on that inference rather than a direct observation.

The results point to both nexioms being needed:
- Norupen alone (test 4) didn't light, so one nexiom isn't enough.
- "At least one lights it" can't fit. Tests 1, 3 and 4 would then leave ditilu as the only possible nexiom, but there must be two.

So with ditilu alone, only one of the two nexioms would be present, and the machine shouldn't light.

PROBE: no
